questions.stem: A pricing method switches over `Object item` with these cases, in this order: `case Number n -> "number";`, then `case Integer i when i > 1000 -> "bulk";`, then `default -> "other";`. It is called with `5000`. What happens?

options.text: The class doesn't compile, since the unguarded `Number` case already takes every `Integer`
options.says: an unguarded case dominates any later case, guarded or not, whose type is a subtype of its own, and javac reports the later one as dominated

options.text: The call returns "bulk", since the `Integer` case is narrower than the `Number` case
options.says: cases are not ranked by how specific they are; order is the only priority, and here the compiler refuses the order

options.text: The call returns "number", since the cases are tried in order and the compiler doesn't evaluate guards
options.says: a guard keeps a case from dominating others, but it doesn't keep the case from being dominated by an earlier unguarded case of a supertype

options.text: The class doesn't compile, since a guarded case must come before every unguarded case of the switch
options.says: only an earlier unguarded case of the same type or a supertype dominates; a guarded case may follow unguarded cases of unrelated types

origin.section: The Compiler Rejects a Case That an Earlier Case Always Wins, but It Does Not Read Guards

questions.stem: `sealed interface Job permits Build, Deploy`, where `Deploy` is a record with a `boolean prod()`. A switch expression over a `Job` has `case Build b -> "run";`, `case Deploy d when d.prod() -> "approve";` and `case Deploy d when !d.prod() -> "run";`, and no `default`. What does javac 21 do?

options.text: It accepts the switch, since between them the two guards accept every `Deploy`
options.says: the compiler doesn't evaluate guards, so it can't see that they complement each other

options.text: It accepts the switch, since `Job` is sealed and each permitted type has a case
options.says: only an unguarded case covers its type; both Deploy cases are guarded

options.text: It refuses the switch, since no case covers `Deploy` without a condition
options.says: a guarded case covers nothing, so Deploy is not covered and the switch expression doesn't cover all possible input values

options.text: It refuses the switch, since two cases for the same type can't both carry a guard
options.says: any number of guarded cases may share a type; the compiler doesn't even check whether they overlap

origin.section: Over a Sealed Type, Naming Every Permitted Subtype Is Exhaustive, and Only Unguarded Cases Count

questions.stem: An audit method uses a switch statement, not an expression, over `Object payload`: `case String s -> log(s);` and `case byte[] bytes -> log(bytes.length + " bytes");`, nothing else. What happens when the class is built and called with an `Integer`?

options.text: It builds, and the `Integer` runs no case, since a switch statement may leave values uncovered
options.says: that holds for a classic statement only; a statement that uses a pattern must be exhaustive like an expression

options.text: It builds, and the `Integer` throws `MatchException`, since javac adds a default that throws
options.says: javac adds that default only to a switch it has already found exhaustive; this one is refused first

options.text: It doesn't build, since a statement with patterns must cover every possible payload
options.says: a switch statement that uses patterns gets the expression's rule: the switch statement does not cover all possible input values

options.text: It doesn't build, since a switch over `Object` must also have a `case null`
options.says: case null plays no part in exhaustiveness; a default or a case Object o would make this switch compile

origin.section: A Switch Statement With Patterns Must Be Exhaustive Too

questions.stem: A settings page renders values with `return switch (value) { case String s -> s; case Object o -> o.toString(); };`. A key in the file has no value, so `value` is `null`. What happens?

options.text: It returns "null", since `case Object o` matches every value the selector can hold
options.says: a type pattern, even case Object o, never matches null; null reaches only case null

options.text: It returns "null", since a switch with a case for every value sends `null` to the last one
options.says: exhaustiveness says nothing about null; without case null a null selector throws before any case is tried

options.text: It throws `NullPointerException` inside the `Object` case, since `o.toString()` is called on `null`
options.says: no case is entered: the switch itself throws on the null selector

options.text: It throws `NullPointerException` before any case, since the switch has no `case null`
options.says: a pattern switch without case null throws NullPointerException on a null selector, whatever its other cases

origin.section: null Matches Only case null; Neither default Nor case Object Does
